guide.title: QR Best Practices & Scannability Guide
guide.subtitle: Everything you need to know about color contrast, error resilience, and high-quality printing.
guide.c1Desc: Optical QR scanners work by sensing contrast between light and dark modules. Always use a dark foreground on a light background or vice-versa. Avoid low contrast combinations like light yellow on white or dark grey on black.
guide.c1Tip1: Foreground should have at least 4:1 contrast ratio against the background.
guide.c1Tip2: Transparent backgrounds work best on white paper or light digital screens.
guide.c2Desc: QR codes use Reed-Solomon error correction to recover damaged or occluded modules.
guide.c2Tip1: Level L (7%): Best for short URLs and simple text where code density should be minimal.
guide.c2Tip2: Level M (15%): Standard for most marketing materials and websites.
guide.c2Tip3: Level Q (25%): Highly recommended whenever embedding small center logos.
guide.c2Tip4: Level H (30%): Maximum redundancy. Required if you cover up to 30% of the center with a logo or print outdoors.
guide.c3Desc: Adding brand logos enhances trust, but remember that the logo covers QR data modules.
guide.c3Tip1: Always keep logo size under 25% of the total QR width.
guide.c3Tip2: Leave 'Excavate' enabled to provide a clean buffer around your logo.
guide.c3Tip3: Always test-scan with both iOS Camera and Android Google Lens before mass printing.
guide.c4Desc: A good rule of thumb for physical prints: Scanning distance should be at most 10 times the width of the QR code.
guide.c4Tip1: Business cards (viewed at 15-30cm): At least 2cm x 2cm (0.8" x 0.8").
guide.c4Tip2: Posters / Flyers (viewed at 1m): At least 10cm x 10cm (4" x 4").
guide.c4Tip3: Export at 2x or 4x resolution for commercial 300 DPI print shops.
